latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Anti-myeloperoxidase ANCA binds membrane-expressed MPO on TNF-primed neutrophils, triggering oxidative burst, degranulation, and NETosis at the endothelial surface. This is the proximal driver of MPA; antibody titer correlates loosely with activity but neutrophil priming determines tissue injury.
Fibrinoid necrosis of arterioles, capillaries, and venules with scant immune complex deposition (pauci-immune on IF). The unifying tissue lesion of MPA across kidney, lung, skin, nerve, and gut.

Focal segmental necrotizing glomerulonephritis with cellular crescents, no significant immune deposits, frequent fibrinoid necrosis. The dominant renal lesion of MPA, presenting as RPGN with active urinary sediment (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, sub-nephrotic proteinuria) and rising creatinine.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Pulmonary capillaritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Neutrophil-mediated destruction of alveolar capillary walls causing intra-alveolar hemorrhage. Manifests as hemoptysis (may be absent in 1/3), diffuse bilateral ground-glass/consolidative infiltrates, dropping hemoglobin, hypoxemia, and increasing DLCO. A defining severe phenotype of MPA carrying the highest acute mortality.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: MPO-ANCA associated interstitial lung disease / pulmonary fibrosis
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: A distinctive chronic UIP- or NSIP-like fibrotic ILD seen disproportionately in MPO-ANCA / MPA, especially in older Japanese patients. May predate vasculitis by years and contributes to long-term mortality independent of vasculitic activity.

Necrotizing vasculitis of small epineurial arteries causing ischemic axonopathy in named peripheral nerves. Presents as asymmetric, painful, stepwise sensorimotor deficits (foot drop, wrist drop), with axonal pattern on EMG and sural biopsy showing vasculitis. Recovery is slow and often incomplete.

Small-vessel cutaneous vasculitis producing palpable purpura predominantly on lower extremities, sometimes with petechiae, livedo, ulcers, or splinter hemorrhages. Reflects systemic small-vessel disease activity but is rarely organ-threatening.
Less common in MPA than in PAN; produces abdominal pain, GI bleeding, mucosal ischemia, and rarely bowel infarction. When present, signals severe systemic disease and increases mortality.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Systemic constitutional cytokine activity (IL-6 / acute phase)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Drives fevers, weight loss, fatigue, arthralgia/myalgia, anorexia, and the elevated CRP/ESR/platelets/normocytic anemia seen in active MPA. Often a prodromal feature for weeks to months before organ-defining disease.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Glomerular sclerosis and tubulointerstitial fibrosis (chronic renal damage)
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Accumulation of globally sclerotic glomeruli and interstitial fibrosis/tubular atrophy from prior crescents. Determines long-term GFR floor and risk of progression to ESRD even after remission. Drives the strong association between baseline creatinine and renal/patient survival.

Combined effect of high-dose glucocorticoids, cyclophosphamide / rituximab-induced B-cell depletion, hypogammaglobulinemia, and lymphopenia. The single largest contributor to first-year mortality in MPA. Particularly drives risk of PJP, severe bacterial infection, HBV reactivation, and herpesvirus reactivation.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Activated, MPO-coated neutrophils degranulate and release NETs at the post-capillary endothelium, producing the fibrinoid necrosis that defines small-vessel vasculitis in MPA.
Glomerular capillary necrosis ruptures Bowman's capsule, allowing fibrin and parietal epithelial cells to form crescents — the histologic substrate of RPGN in MPA.
Alveolar capillary necrosis allows red cells to spill into alveoli, producing diffuse alveolar hemorrhage.
Necrotizing inflammation of epineurial arterioles ischemically damages individual nerve trunks, generating mononeuritis multiplex.
Postcapillary venule vasculitis in dermal vessels manifests as palpable purpura, particularly dependent areas.
Mesenteric small-vessel involvement causes mucosal ischemia, abdominal pain and GI bleeding when present.
Innate immune activation drives IL-6, TNF, and acute-phase response, producing the prodromal constitutional syndrome.
Loss of functional glomeruli to crescents and necrosis produces a rapid rise in creatinine — the hallmark of RPGN in MPA.
Falling GFR raises BUN in parallel with creatinine; uremia drives later anorexia and pericarditis.
Glomerular capillary breaks let dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts into the urine — an early and highly sensitive marker of glomerular vasculitis.
Active sediment with dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and proteinuria is the hallmark of crescentic GN.
Crescentic GN typically produces sub-nephrotic proteinuria (UPCR 0.5–3 g/g); frank nephrotic-range protein is unusual and suggests overlap or another process.
UPCR rises into the 0.5–3 g/g range typical of pauci-immune crescentic GN.
Crescentic GN is a leading cause of dialysis-requiring AKI in adults; without prompt induction therapy, half of severely affected kidneys progress to ESRD.
Healed crescents become globally sclerotic glomeruli; tubulointerstitial fibrosis follows nephron loss. Determines residual GFR.
Intra-alveolar hemorrhage acutely lowers hemoglobin, often by 2–4 g/dL within days. A falling Hb without external blood loss is a major clue to occult DAH.
Alveolar filling with blood produces V/Q mismatch and shunt physiology, dropping SpO2 and driving respiratory failure.
Hypoxemia and rising work of breathing produce tachypnea.

Alveolar hemorrhage produces bilateral central ground-glass and consolidation indistinguishable on imaging from pneumonia or pulmonary edema; bronchoscopy with sequential BAL aliquots showing increasing bloodiness is the bedside discriminator.
Pulmonary or airway involvement can cause cough.
Capillaritis is the immediate substrate; severe DAH carries 25–50% short-term mortality without rapid immunosuppression.
Severe DAH can progress to bilateral infiltrates and severe hypoxemic failure meeting ARDS criteria.
Asymmetric multifocal nerve infarction produces foot drop, wrist drop, painful sensory loss in named-nerve distributions.
Dermal venulitis classically produces palpable purpura on the lower extremities.
Intestinal mucosal ischemia produces post-prandial abdominal pain and, in severe cases, bowel infarction.
Cytokine-driven low-grade fevers are common in active MPA, sometimes the only initial sign.
Anorexia and chronic inflammation produce significant weight loss, often >5 kg over the prodromal period.
Cytokine illness and anemia of inflammation produce profound fatigue.
Diffuse myalgias frequent in active MPA; may mimic polymyalgia rheumatica.
Non-erosive arthralgia/arthritis of large and small joints occurs in roughly half of patients.
IL-6-driven hepatic acute-phase response raises CRP, often markedly (50–200 mg/L) in active MPA.
ESR rises along with CRP and fibrinogen during active vasculitis.
Reactive thrombocytosis is typical of active MPA, distinguishing it from TTP/HUS or DIC where platelets fall.
Anemia of inflammation contributes to a normocytic anemia; in DAH or renal failure the drop is steeper and added on top.
Mild-moderate leukocytosis is typical, eosinophilia is generally absent (a key contrast with EGPA).
Residual scarring fixes baseline creatinine at a higher level even after vasculitic remission, driving long-term CKD.
Nephron loss and renin activation produce sustained hypertension that itself accelerates further GFR decline.
Progressive fibrotic ILD reduces diffusion capacity and produces chronic, exertional then resting hypoxemia.
Chronic dry cough is a predominant symptom of MPA-associated UIP/NSIP-pattern ILD.

Combined glucocorticoid + cyclophosphamide / rituximab regimens substantially raise risk of bacterial pneumonia, PJP, herpes zoster, and HBV reactivation; first-year mortality from infection rivals mortality from active vasculitis.
Severe DAH is among the most lethal acute presentations of MPA and strongly raises early mortality hazard.
Severity of renal failure (especially dialysis dependence at presentation) is a leading independent predictor of long-term mortality.
Severe infection during induction is the single largest non-vasculitic cause of death in the first year after diagnosis.
Progressive fibrotic ILD is a major late cause of death in MPO-ANCA disease, particularly in older Japanese cohorts.
MPO-ANCA positivity is the serologic expression of the dominant MPA ANCA phenotype.
The disease can present with persistent or recurrent fever over the observed clinical history.
MPA pulmonary capillaritis or ILD can mimic pneumonia but does not respond to antibacterial therapy.
Pulmonary, cardiac, serosal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement can cause dyspnea.

axes.shape_free_text: High-titer MPO-ANCA at presentation in ~70% of MPA. Falls (often to undetectable) with effective induction. A persistent rise during follow-up roughly doubles short-term relapse risk but is not a sole indication to escalate therapy.
Typically negative or low in MPA; positive PR3-ANCA points away from MPA toward GPA, although ~10% of MPA may be PR3-ANCA positive.
Perinuclear (p-ANCA) IIF pattern positive in most MPA cases, in conjunction with anti-MPO ELISA positivity.
Birmingham Vasculitis Activity Score; a composite organ-system activity index used to grade severity at presentation and during follow-up. Active MPA usually scores 10–30.

Rises rapidly (often doubling within days–weeks) in RPGN. Peak value at presentation is the dominant prognostic axis for renal and patient survival. After induction, partial recovery over 1–6 months; many patients are left with a higher new baseline.
Tracks creatinine; uremic symptoms (anorexia, pericarditis, encephalopathy) appear when BUN exceeds ~80–100 mg/dL.

Dysmorphic glomerular hematuria, often with RBC casts. Highly sensitive and an early sign of glomerular vasculitis. Persistent microscopic hematuria after induction is a relative marker of ongoing renal activity.
Composite of dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts, and proteinuria; the bedside discriminator for glomerular vs non-glomerular renal disease.
Sub-nephrotic proteinuria typical (1–3 g/day); nephrotic-range protein is unusual and should raise concern for an alternative or overlapping glomerulopathy.
Typical UPCR 0.5–3 g/g during active disease.
Falls in oliguric crescentic GN; oliguria/anuria predicts dialysis need.
Normocytic anemia from inflammation, renal failure, and (when DAH present) acute alveolar blood loss. A rapid drop without external bleeding should prompt evaluation for occult DAH.
Reactive thrombocytosis (often 400–800 × 10^9/L) typical in active MPA. Thrombocytopenia is uncommon and should redirect toward TTP/HUS, DIC, drug effect, or HLH.
Mild-moderate neutrophilic leukocytosis. Eosinophilia is generally absent; >10% eosinophils should redirect toward EGPA.
Elevated during active disease; falls during cyclophosphamide therapy and is a key dosing/monitoring axis (target nadir typically >2.0 × 10^9/L).
Markedly elevated (often 50–200 mg/L) in active disease; falls within days–weeks of induction. Persistent elevation during apparent clinical remission is concerning for occult activity or infection.
Often >50–100 mm/hr in active vasculitis; lags CRP in falling.
Typically NORMAL in pauci-immune MPA — a key discriminator from immune-complex GN (lupus nephritis, cryoglobulinemic GN, post-infectious GN, MPGN). Low C3 should redirect the differential.
Typically normal in MPA; low C4 should redirect toward immune-complex disease.
May be weakly positive (low titer, non-specific). Strongly positive ANA, especially with anti-dsDNA, redirects to lupus.
Frequently positive at low–moderate titer in MPA; non-specific.
Palpable purpura on lower extremities is the classic skin finding; less commonly nodules, ulcers, splinter hemorrhages.
Asymmetric, painful, stepwise sensorimotor deficits in named-nerve distributions (mononeuritis multiplex; foot drop, wrist drop, painful sensory loss). Recovery slow and often incomplete.
Dry or productive cough as a symptom axis; mechanism depends on pulmonary, airway, cardiac, or mediastinal involvement.
Frank hemoptysis is present in only ~2/3 of DAH; absence does NOT exclude DAH. Bronchoscopy with sequential BAL aliquots showing increasing bloodiness is the bedside diagnostic standard.
Falls acutely in DAH, sometimes severely; in chronic MPA-ILD declines slowly over years with exertional desaturation.
Tachypnea in DAH or ARDS phase.

In DAH: bilateral central ground-glass and consolidation, often perihilar, sparing apices/costophrenic angles. In MPA-ILD: chronic basal-predominant reticulation, traction bronchiectasis, honeycombing (UIP-like).
Often elevated due to renal involvement; may fall acutely if hemorrhagic shock from DAH or sepsis from immunosuppression. Long-term hypertension drives further GFR decline.
Often hypertensive at presentation due to renal involvement; chronic uncontrolled hypertension is a major modifiable accelerator of CKD.
Often mildly tachycardic in active disease; tachycardia rises sharply in DAH or sepsis.
Low-grade fever common; high spiking fever should redirect attention to infection.
Significant prodromal weight loss (often >5 kg over 1–3 months) is common.
Profound fatigue is one of the earliest and most persistent symptoms.
Diffuse myalgia common in active MPA; distinguishable from PMR by prominent multisystem involvement.
Non-erosive oligo/polyarthritis or arthralgia in roughly half of patients; typically migratory.
Less common than in PAN; suggests mesenteric small-vessel involvement and signals severe disease.
Per-day hazard of dialysis-requiring AKI; very high during the first weeks of untreated/under-treated MPA.
Per-day hazard of severe DAH event; mortality in severe DAH approaches 25–50% without rapid immunosuppression and consideration of plasma exchange.
Hazard of progression to severe hypoxemic respiratory failure in DAH or superimposed infection.
Combined hazard of bacterial pneumonia, PJP, herpes zoster, sepsis. Highest during first 3–6 months of induction; PJP risk concentrated in high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide window.
Elevated when receiving rituximab or high-dose glucocorticoids in HBsAg+ or anti-HBc+ patients; mandates HBV screening before induction and antiviral prophylaxis when indicated.
Latent TB and HBV/HCV reactivation risk under prolonged immunosuppression; screen with IGRA, HBsAg/anti-HBc, anti-HCV before induction.
Endocarditis (especially HACEK, Bartonella) can produce ANCA positivity and pauci-immune GN, mimicking MPA. This must be excluded with blood cultures and TTE before committing to immunosuppression.
Dose adjustment required for cyclophosphamide, TMP-SMX, and many supportive drugs in CKD; relevant axis through induction and maintenance.

Aggregate per-day mortality hazard from DAH, severe AKI, severe infection during induction, and long-term ILD/CKD. 1-year mortality historically 10–20% in modern cohorts; 5-year mortality 25–35% with infection and chronic renal failure as the leading causes.
MPO-ANCA positivity is the dominant MPA serologic pattern.
PR3-ANCA positivity can occur in a minority of MPA but points less strongly to MPA than MPO-ANCA.
C-ANCA pattern is less typical for MPA than p-ANCA/MPO patterns.
History-level fever burden over days to months, distinct from a single measured body temperature.

axes.display_name: Lack of clinical response to standard antibacterial therapy
axes.shape_free_text: Persistent fever, inflammation, or organ findings despite antibacterial therapy that should have covered ordinary bacterial infection.
Patient-reported or observed breathlessness from pulmonary, cardiac, mediastinal, anemia, or systemic inflammatory involvement.

axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Creatinine and BUN both reflect falling GFR in renal MPA; tightly co-vary except when prerenal physiology or upper GI bleeding raises BUN disproportionately.
Crescentic GN with falling GFR produces oliguria/anuria as creatinine rises.
Higher and rapidly rising creatinine raises the per-day hazard of dialysis requirement.
Capillaritis activity is the proximate determinant of severe DAH events.
Rapidly falling hemoglobin in a patient with bilateral infiltrates and hypoxemia is a high-prior signal for ongoing DAH.
Cumulative immunosuppression burden tracks closely with serious infection per-day hazard.
Both rise with IL-6 driven acute phase response; ESR lags CRP both up and down.
IL-6 drives reactive thrombocytosis, in contrast to TTP/HUS/DIC where platelets fall — a useful discriminator.
ELISA anti-MPO and IIF p-ANCA pattern are usually concordant in MPA.
Baseline creatinine at presentation (and dialysis dependence) is the most consistent independent predictor of long-term mortality in MPA.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe DAH and rapidly progressive renal disease are the canonical indications for IV pulse methylprednisolone (typically 500–1000 mg/day × 3 days).
Untreated endocarditis or other infection mimicking ANCA vasculitis must be excluded before pulsing steroids.

side_effects.interpretation: infection risk amplified during and after pulse
rises in BP from mineralocorticoid effect

treatments.context_specific_role: Used as initial pulse for organ-threatening MPA (DAH, RPGN with rapid creatinine rise, severe mononeuritis multiplex), bridging until cyclophosphamide or rituximab takes effect.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oral prednisolone (typically 1 mg/kg/day, max 60–80 mg) follows pulse therapy and is the backbone of induction; modern PEXIVAS-informed practice supports a faster taper to limit infection risk.

side_effects.interpretation: dose-dependent infection risk; PJP risk above ~20 mg/day prednisolone for >4 weeks

treatments.context_specific_role: Backbone induction and tapered maintenance immunosuppression; PEXIVAS reduced-dose regimen is increasingly standard. Avacopan-containing regimens allow further steroid sparing.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Cyclophosphamide (CYCLOPS regimen — IV pulse 15 mg/kg q2–3 weeks, dose-adjusted for renal function and age) achieves remission in ~80–90% of severe MPA. Equivalent to rituximab in non-inferiority trials (RAVE, RITUXVAS).
Cytopenia from prior dosing requires dose reduction or delay.
In patients of reproductive age, cumulative CYC dose causes ovarian failure and azoospermia; rituximab is preferred.

side_effects.interpretation: infection risk amplified, especially with concurrent steroids

treatments.context_specific_role: Induction therapy for severe organ-threatening MPA. Co-administered with mesna for IV pulses to protect the bladder. Cumulative dose <25 g desired to limit malignancy risk.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Rituximab (375 mg/m² weekly × 4 or 1 g × 2 doses) depletes CD20+ B cells, reducing pathogenic ANCA production. Non-inferior to cyclophosphamide for induction (RAVE, RITUXVAS) and superior for relapsing disease.
Mandatory HBsAg/anti-HBc screening prior to rituximab; antiviral prophylaxis required for HBsAg+ and considered for isolated anti-HBc+.
Preferred over cyclophosphamide in patients of reproductive age.

side_effects.interpretation: B-cell depletion and hypogammaglobulinemia raise infection risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Induction and maintenance (MAINRITSAN, RITAZAREM). Particularly preferred in young patients, women of reproductive age, prior cyclophosphamide exposure, and relapsing disease.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PEXIVAS (NEJM 2020) showed no overall benefit on death/ESRD at 7 PLEX sessions but selected guidelines still endorse PLEX for life-threatening DAH and selected severe AKI; an individualized risk–benefit decision.
Routine PLEX did NOT reduce death/ESRD even in severe renal disease in PEXIVAS, narrowing its indication to selected cases.

side_effects.interpretation: transient hypofibrinogenemia after multiple PLEX sessions
central line and immunoglobulin removal raise infection risk

treatments.context_specific_role: Selective rescue for life-threatening DAH or, with reservations post-PEXIVAS, severe AKI with high crescent burden in dialysis-dependent presentations.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Avacopan (ADVOCATE trial, NEJM 2021) blocks C5aR-mediated neutrophil priming, allowing substantial steroid reduction with non-inferior remission and improved sustained remission and eGFR recovery at 52 weeks.
Hepatotoxicity is the major signal toxicity; avoid in significant baseline liver disease.

side_effects.interpretation: asymptomatic LFT rise — monitor; discontinue if persistently elevated

treatments.context_specific_role: Steroid-sparing component of induction in combination with rituximab or cyclophosphamide; major value is reduction of glucocorticoid burden and the associated infection / metabolic toxicity.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Azathioprine (2 mg/kg/day) post-CYC induction maintains remission (CYCAZAREM); non-inferior to MMF and inferior to rituximab in MAINRITSAN.

treatments.context_specific_role: Maintenance therapy after CYC induction; cheaper and oral but inferior to rituximab for relapse prevention. Check TPMT/NUDT15 prior to start.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Fixed-interval rituximab maintenance (500 mg q6 months for 18–24 months; MAINRITSAN, RITAZAREM) reduces relapse vs azathioprine.

side_effects.interpretation: cumulative B-cell depletion and IgG decline

treatments.context_specific_role: Preferred maintenance therapy in MPO-ANCA MPA after rituximab or cyclophosphamide induction.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: MMF is an alternative to azathioprine for maintenance and may be considered for selected non-severe induction in MPO-ANCA disease (MYCYC trial showed inferiority vs cyclophosphamide for relapse but not for initial remission).
Strong teratogen; contraindicated in pregnancy.

treatments.context_specific_role: Alternative maintenance immunosuppressant when azathioprine intolerant or contraindicated.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: PJP prophylaxis (single-strength daily or DS three times weekly) is mandatory for any combination of high-dose steroid + cyclophosphamide or rituximab; PJP risk is highest in the first 6 months of induction.

side_effects.interpretation: competitive inhibition of tubular secretion; not true GFR drop

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard PJP and incidental gram-positive/some gram-negative prophylaxis throughout induction and early maintenance.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: RAS blockade reduces proteinuria and slows CKD progression in residual MPA-related glomerulopathy.
Use with care in advanced CKD or hemodynamic instability; expect a 10–20% creatinine bump on initiation.

treatments.context_specific_role: Long-term renoprotection and BP control after vasculitic remission.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Indicated for refractory hyperkalemia, fluid overload, uremic complications, or severe metabolic acidosis. ~25% of dialysis-dependent presentations recover renal function with intensive immunosuppression.

treatments.context_specific_role: Bridge or definitive support in dialysis-dependent AKI from MPA.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Severe DAH frequently progresses to hypoxemic respiratory failure requiring intubation; lung-protective ventilation strategy applies.

treatments.context_specific_role: Life support during severe DAH-driven respiratory failure.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis prophylaxis is standard given the prolonged steroid course; calcium/vit D ± bisphosphonate per FRAX risk.

treatments.context_specific_role: Standard supportive care during prolonged glucocorticoid therapy.

japanese_or_east_asian.trajectory_modulation: MPO-ANCA dominant; higher prevalence of MPA-associated ILD; relative MPA:GPA ratio inverted compared with Northern Europe

northern_european.trajectory_modulation: PR3-ANCA / GPA dominant in this population

HLA-DQ_associated_with_MPO_ANCA.trajectory_modulation: HLA-DQ alleles are the strongest GWAS signal for MPO-ANCA disease, distinct from HLA-DPB1*04:01 in PR3-ANCA disease, supporting MPO- and PR3-ANCA disease as genetically distinct entities

high_silica_exposure_history.trajectory_modulation: consistent epidemiologic association with ANCA-associated vasculitis, particularly MPO-ANCA / MPA

hydralazine_high_dose_long_term.trajectory_modulation: drug-induced MPO-ANCA vasculitis frequently with high titer, often with anti-LAMP-2 / anti-elastase / anti-histone reactivity; tends to remit on drug withdrawal

propylthiouracil_methimazole.trajectory_modulation: antithyroid drugs are classic triggers of MPO-ANCA vasculitis

levamisole_contaminated_cocaine.trajectory_modulation: cutaneous-predominant ANCA vasculitis with retiform purpura

minocycline.trajectory_modulation: drug-induced ANCA vasculitis, often with low-titer ANA positivity

interstitial_lung_disease_present.trajectory_modulation: ILD may predate vasculitis by years in MPO-ANCA disease and significantly worsens long-term prognosis

current_smoker.trajectory_modulation: modest contribution; smoking is a stronger risk for PR3-ANCA / GPA than for MPA

supportive_care: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis against PJP throughout induction and at least the first 3–6 months of maintenance, especially during steroid + CYC or rituximab therapy
Glucocorticoid-induced osteoporosis prevention with calcium, vitamin D, and bisphosphonate per fracture risk; bone density baseline and follow-up DXA
Mesna co-administration with IV cyclophosphamide and aggressive hydration to prevent hemorrhagic cystitis
Anti-emetic prophylaxis with cyclophosphamide infusions

Vaccination review and update before initiating immunosuppression: pneumococcal (PCV + PPSV), influenza annually, recombinant zoster (Shingrix), SARS-CoV-2 boosters; complete live vaccines BEFORE rituximab if possible

HBV (HBsAg, anti-HBc, anti-HBs), HCV, HIV, IGRA/PPD, and strongyloides serology screening before induction; antiviral prophylaxis (entecavir/tenofovir) for HBsAg+ or isolated anti-HBc+ patients receiving rituximab or high-dose steroids
Strict blood pressure control with ACE inhibitor or ARB (target generally <130/80 mmHg) for renoprotection and to reduce long-term GFR loss
Tight glycemic monitoring during high-dose steroid course; treat steroid-induced diabetes

Fertility counseling and preservation (sperm banking, oocyte/embryo cryopreservation, GnRH agonist co-administration with cyclophosphamide) before cyclophosphamide in patients of reproductive age; preferentially use rituximab
Bronchoscopy with serial BAL when DAH is suspected, both diagnostically (sequentially bloodier aliquots) and to exclude superimposed infection

Renal biopsy at presentation to confirm pauci-immune crescentic GN, exclude immune-complex GN and anti-GBM disease (dual-positive ANCA + anti-GBM occurs in ~5–10%), and grade chronicity (Berden histopathologic classification informs prognosis)
Anti-GBM antibody testing alongside ANCA in any RPGN-DAH presentation, as dual positivity occurs and changes management urgency
Echocardiography and blood cultures in suspected MPA cases to rule out infective endocarditis as an ANCA-mimic before committing to immunosuppression
Nutrition support and SLP/PT mobilization during prolonged hospitalization
Stress ulcer prophylaxis (PPI) during high-dose steroid course in critically ill patients
VTE prophylaxis given high thrombotic risk in active vasculitis, particularly in DAH or nephrotic-range proteinuria, balanced against bleeding risk

Long-term surveillance: serial creatinine, urinalysis with sediment, MPO-ANCA titer trend, BVAS, pulmonary function tests (especially DLCO) for ILD progression, and bladder cancer screening in patients with cumulative cyclophosphamide exposure
Smoking cessation, particularly important when MPA-associated ILD coexists

Patient education on relapse warning signs (return of constitutional symptoms, hematuria, hemoptysis, new neurologic deficit, palpable purpura) and on infection signs requiring urgent evaluation during immunosuppression
Multidisciplinary follow-up coordination among nephrology, rheumatology, pulmonology, and primary care for long-term management
